hook.line: The year King Alfonso X of Castile had its rules written in his “Book of Games” — the ancestor of checkers and fanorona.
hook.say: Let me tell you the story of the ancestor.

p: The name comes from Arabic “al-qirq”, and “qirkat” appears in the 10th-century “Book of Songs”.
Through Islamic Spain it reached Europe, and it is thought to have sparked the birth of checkers.

ch.say: It is the parent of many games.
tl: Similar boards carved on an Egyptian temple roof (date uncertain)
Meets the chessboard and leads to checkers
Rules recorded in Alfonso X’s Book of Games
Still kept alive as a traditional game in Spain and elsewhere

ch.say: Move along the lines and jump to capture.
ch.cap: A 5×5 grid of points and lines; 12 stones each, only the centre empty
p: Stones move along a line to the next empty point, and capture by jumping.
Chained jumps, just like checkers — many games grew from here.

cards: A descendant said to be born on the chessboard
A descendant on a 9×5 board with unique captures
A similar capturing game on a bow-tie board

ch.say: It survives in a beautiful medieval book.
cards: The “Wise King” of Castile, who had chess, tables and more recorded with lavish illustrations
A priceless manuscript of medieval games, kept at the Escorial monastery in Spain

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: The Arabic article “the” — as in alcohol and alkali
Can you draw the board on the ground?
Yes — lines and pebbles are enough, one reason it survived
Strong players are said to draw often

ch.say: Take on the wisdom of the ancestors!
p: Puzzle over the same board people played a thousand years ago.
